value: Chatbots accept free text input, VAs accept speech input; multi-turn dialogues with clarifying questions ('Tell me more', 'Why do you say that?') and empathetic reactions ('I am sorry to hear that'); conversations begin with greetings/mood check-ins; users can complete suggested activities
quotes:
“the conversational design of these two Chatbots allows users to communicate using free text input”
“Chatbots are designed to support multi-turn dialogues, engaging in clarifications such as "Tell me more", and "Why do you say that?". They also offer empathetic reactions (e.g., "I am sorry to hear that").”
“The two Chatbots began their conversations with greetings, pleasantries, or mood check-ins ("Hi <NAME>, how are you feeling?").”
“Their responses are also less dependent on search, using customized content throughout conversations”

title: Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks of Generative AI Mental-Health Chatbots: A Systematic Review and Regulatory Framework.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Generative AI systems produce open-ended responses that adapt dynamically to user input, enabling flexible interactions. Multi-turn conversational interaction is dominant. No specific details on response length, tone, persona, relational style, reflection/summarisation, or opportunities to skip/revise/stop.
quotes: “generative AI systems produce open-ended responses that adapt dynamically to user input, enabling flexible interactions while introducing new and underexplored challenges related to safety, privacy, and cybersecurity.”
country: USA (review); included studies span multiple countries including USA, CHN, AUS, CAN, NZL, POL, KOR, ZAF
age_as_reported: adolescents or young adults (2/33, 6.1%); general/mixed populations across included studies

title: Co-developing a Mental Health and Wellbeing Chatbot With and for Young People.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input: free-text and menu-based. Open-ended and constrained dialogue. Conversational style with emojis, jokes, GIFs, storytelling. Persona: 'Ash', gender-neutral robot, friendly, funny, empathic, humorous, inspiring, charismatic. Users can stop, access menu, choose topics. If chatbot does not understand, it asks a question or lets user know.
quotes:
“The implementation for this was be as simple as keyword detection (e.g., hello, thanks, nice, great, swear words), and train a model to detect the longer phrases like how are you, who made you)”
“It uses emojis, jokes and gifs, a more conversational style of asking questions, storytelling to create a bot persona”
“A "menu" also was provided to bring up a list of ways the participant can interact with the chatbot”
“Ash is the guide, it is inspiring and charismatic, fun, friendly, empathic, humorous (See Figure 1). It uses emojis, jokes and gifs, a more conversational style of asking questions, storytelling to create a bot persona”
“If the chatbot did not understand the intent of the message then it would ask a question or let the participant know they did not understand.”
age_as_reported: 15–17 years of age

title: Behavior Emotion Therapy System and You: Co-Design and Evaluation of a Mental Health Chatbot and Digital Human for Mild to Moderate Anxiety in Healthy Participants.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Two input modes: free-text for the text-only chatbot and voice-only for the digital human. Dialog-tree based with keyword matching; constrained dialogue with pre-authored responses. Persona: female-presenting, named BETSY, semiformal tone ('like an acquaintance'), empathetic, soft-voiced. Users found responses 'excessively lengthy' and 'overly talkative.' External links redirected users out of the chat interface.
quotes:
“BETSY was provided with a soft-voice tone, slowing down the pace of her speech”
“Both groups found BETSY overly talkative and her responses excessively lengthy.”
“The most disruptive aspect was redirecting users to external webpages for relaxation exercises and information”
“It should be somewhat formal like an acquaintance”
loc: Results Phase 2, p.8; Results Phase 3, p.9; Table 1, p.4

title: Chatbot-Delivered Cognitive Behavioral Therapy in Adolescents With Depression and Anxiety During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Feasibility and Acceptability Study.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input: emoji selection from default menu of 19 moods plus free-text emotion words and self-selected emoji; conversational agent checks in and offers psychoeducation and tools; lesson acceptability rated on binary scale (thumbs up/down); mood impact after tool utilization reported as feeling same, better, or worse; relational tone with user informed they are talking to a robot
quotes:
“The user experience is centered around mood tracking and goal-oriented, tailored conversations”
“In-the-moment emotional state was reported through emoji selection with a default menu of 19 total moods, including options for negative (angry, sad, and anxious), positive (happy and content), and average mood (okay), with an additional ability to type in free text emotion words and self-selected emoji expressions.”
“Safety features include informing the user they are talking to a robot and not a real person”
age_as_reported: 13 to 17 years

title: Too good to be true? Exploring the role of artificial intelligence chatbots in treating depression and anxiety.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Conversational chatbots using natural language processing to simulate human-like dialogue. Some use empathetic language (Caro, Emma); others act as care receivers to foster self-compassion (Vincent, Gloomy, Perla). Platforms integrate mood tracking, automated check-ins, and structured therapeutic activities.
quotes:
“AI chatbots operate through natural language processing and machine learning, which enable them to understand conversational context and simulate human-like interactions”
“some chatbots, such as Caro and Emma, use empathetic language to deepen engagement. Others, like Vincent, Gloomy, and Perla, act as care receivers, encouraging users to provide support, which fosters self-compassion”
age_as_reported: adolescents and young adults

title: A Clinical Quality-Assurance Panel for Patient-Facing Black-Box Large Language Models in Healthcare: Anchored Forced-Choice Drift Monitoring for Sensitive Communication.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Constrained forced-choice dialogue: model presented with two labeled items and must choose which is harder. Output restricted to one-line JSON with trial_id, choice (A or B), and confidence (integer 0-100). No free-text generation permitted. Prompt explicitly excludes emotional valence, moral desirability, and clinical importance from the comparison.
quotes:
“Each trial presented two labeled items (A and B) and asked the model to imagine them as same-sized solid materials. The task was to choose which item was harder”
“Return exactly one line of JSON and no other text: {"trial_id":"[TRIAL_ID]","choice":"A" or "B","confidence":[integer 0-100]}.”

title: Barriers and Facilitators to the Use of Large Language Model-Based Conversational Agents in Mental Healthcare: A Systematic Review.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Primarily free-text conversational interaction. Repetitive responses reported as a barrier (15/27, 56%). Scholich et al. found chatbots asked significantly fewer elaborative questions than therapists (U = 9, p = 0.001). Inability to detect nonverbal cues noted (17/27, 63%). Artificial empathy critiqued as potentially superficial. Voice-based interaction available in some agents (Clare, WarmGPT).
quotes:
“repetitive responses (k = 15, 56%)”
“chatbots asked significantly fewer elaborative questions (U = 9, p = 0.001)”
“Inability to detect nonverbal cues (k = 17, 63%)”
“The concept of artificial empathy has been critiqued as potentially superficial”
country: USA, CHN, GBR, AUS, DEU, ISR, JPN, KOR, SAU, ESP, SWE

title: AI-Facilitated Cognitive Reappraisal via Socrates 2.0: Mixed Methods Feasibility Study.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Text-based conversational interface with Socratic questioning style; open-ended, reflective questions; context-sensitive responses generated by LLM rather than predetermined answers; focus on cognitive reappraisal
quotes:
“Socrates 2.0 generates unique, context-sensitive responses based on the user's input.”
“An LLM-based tool differs greatly from traditional rule-based CBT apps that rely on predetermined answers that are given verbatim after prespecified user inputs.”
age_as_reported: at least aged 18 years; mean age 39.9 (SD 15.50) years

title: Use of Artificial Intelligence in Mental Healthcare, Health Psychology, and Related Research: A Narrative Review to Address Challenges and Opportunities.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: ChatGPT described as having 'advanced problem‐solving and conversational capabilities.' AI-based psychology apps described as 'judgment‐free.' ICAs noted for patients revealing 'personal information more freely, establishing a better relationship.' Conversational AI described as able to 'engage in conversations with patients, gather information, and provide interventions.' No details on input format, response length, or specific conversational design parameters.
quotes:
“ChatGPT, a new browser‐based AI service, has seen widespread attention due to its advanced problem‐solving and conversational capabilities”
“Speaking with an AI designed to be judgment‐free and with similar knowledge to a professional may be extremely reassuring”
“the patients tend to reveal personal information more freely, establishing a better relationship and allowing the ICAs to learn and achieve ABC”
“Conversational AI can engage in conversations with patients, gather information, and provide interventions based on the evidence gathered”

title: Breaking Barriers in Student Mental Health Care With AI-Enhanced Group Cognitive Behavioral Therapy: Pilot Feasibility Study.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Text-based free-text chatbot interaction via web browser. Dashboard displaying chatbot interface and archived conversations. Participants could share specific exchanges with therapist or flag conversations as inappropriate. Tone described as informal and friendly. Qualitative feedback: participants felt it was like talking to a friend, structured analysis of situations; but some found responses impersonal, repetitive, lacking empathy.
quotes:
“The front end, delivered via the user's web browser, allowed participants to interact with the chatbot and review archived conversations.”
“Participants accessed a dashboard displaying the CBT ChatBot's interface and archived conversations, with options to share specific exchanges with their therapist or to flag conversations perceived as inappropriate”
“I felt like I was talking to a friend. And I even noticed a useful dissection and analysis of the situation, greater than a friend would have offered.”
“our chatbot communicated in Romanian and assumed a relatively informal, friendly tone that suited our sample”
loc: Methods, The Intervention Program; Results, Qualitative Analyses; Discussion, Limitations
age_as_reported: university students aged 18 years and older; mean age 22.06, SD 1.78 years

title: Impact of Conversational and Animation Features of a Mental Health App Virtual Agent on Depressive Symptoms and User Experience Among College Students: randomized Controlled Trial
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input: speech-to-text for user verbal input (conversational condition only); TTS for agent dialogue. Question-and-response style dialogue embedded within CBT modules. Microphone icon as visual cue (red=on, white=off). Nonconversational condition: no user input allowed. Agent persona: 'virtual coach'. Animation condition included human-like nonverbal body movements, mouth movements, gestures; nonanimated was static with blank expression.
quotes:
“The conversational feature was characterized by user-agent interactivity in whcih question-and-response style dialogue was embedded within the CBT modules. The virtual agent asked questions or instructed the participant to complete activities aloud.”
“A microphone icon provided a visual cue for users to engage in conversation with the agent when red, the microphone is on, and white when off.”
“The nonconversational condition did not allow the user to add their input or respond to questions.”
“The animated condition included human-like nonverbal body movements, mouth movements, and gestures in association with the information provided by the virtual agent. The nonanimated condition displayed a static, nonmoving virtual agent with a blank facial expression.”
age_as_reported: 18-30 years; college students; mean age 19.97 years (SD 2.19)

title: Intelligent virtual agents in psychotherapy: a safety evaluation across high-risk mental health scenarios.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Free-form spoken input via speech-to-text; open-ended dialogue (conversations flow naturally after initial scripted prompt). Turn-taking managed by red/green microphone indicator. The system prompt instructs short, naturally sounding sentences, formal address, empathy, and appropriate interpersonal interaction style. The avatar resembles a male psychiatrist with lip sync technology. German language communication.
quotes:
“Google's speech-to-text (STT) service was used to transcribe what the users were saying”
“the transcription was sent to OpenAI's large language model GPT-4omni, which answered the query, again in textual form.”
“use short, naturally sounding sentences”
“Address the user formally”
“Show empathy and an appropriate interpersonal interaction style, avoiding offensive or escalating statements”
“a red or green microphone indicated to the participants when it was their turn to talk”
“Participants saw a close-up of the IVA's face that was designed to resemble a male psychiatrist”
“The whole communication was taking place in German”
age_as_reported: Testers: mean age 39 years (SD=9.90); Raters: mean age 32 years (SD=1.41). All licensed psychotherapists.

title: Evaluating Generative AI in Mental Health: Systematic Review of Capabilities and Limitations
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Primarily question-and-answer format with zero-shot prompting (single prompt input, single response output). One study allowed free user interaction with ChatGPT on personal devices. No menu-based input, constrained dialogue, response length controls, persona design, or reflection/summarisation features described. Users could not skip, revise, or choose pathways in most studies.
quotes:
“The single-task (eg, question and answer format) evaluation format in the studies prevents the studies from drawing conclusions on LLM performance on a combination of clinical skills.”
“individuals accessed ChatGPT-3.5 on their own personal devices”
loc: Discussion - Principal Findings; Results - User-Involved Evaluation

title: Therapy chatbots and emotional complexity: do therapy chatbots really empathise?. [Review]
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Text-based chat interaction. Users can chat with the app, enter and track emotions. Interactions are described as not being reciprocal interpersonal dialogues. Longer written responses may be perceived as more empathetic.
quotes:
“Users can chat with the app, enter and track their emotions over time, and practise skills and techniques such as mindfulness, meditation, and journaling”
“interactions with chatbots are not actual dialogues: they are not reciprocal, interpersonal interactions”
“A longer written response may be perceived as more empathetic by informants”
loc: Introduction p.1, Empathy section p.4, Risks section p.3

title: Feasibility and User Experience of an AI-Supported mHealth Intervention for Remote Life Goal Setting Based on Flow Theory: Exploratory Within-Participant Study.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Text-based chatbot interaction. Structured dialogue following R-ACS steps with initial questions, rating collection, and feedback. AI persona is 'supportive coach tone.' AI displays both user-assessed and AI-assessed CS ratings and prompts reflective dialogue on discrepancies. Free-text explanations collected from participants. OT condition used standardized script for initial questions and feedback structure. AI outputs were reformatted by researchers to match standardized OT format to minimize presentation bias.
quotes:
“Participant ratings of challenge and skill levels (each on a 7-point scale), along with free-text explanations of their ratings”
“The AI displayed both user-assessed and AI-assessed CS ratings, prompting reflective dialogue when discrepancies were noted”
“the persona (supportive coach tone)”
“the OT followed a strict, structured guide adhering to the same R-ACS steps”
“The therapist used a standardized script for the initial questions and feedback structure”
loc: Methods, Procedure and AI-Supported mHealth Intervention sections; Methods, Prompt Structure and Safety, p.4; Methods, Intervention Flow, p.4; Discussion, p.7
age_as_reported: aged between 20 and 76 years

title: Optimizing personalized psychological well-being interventions through digital phenotyping: results from a randomized non-clinical trial
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input with Likert-scale numeric responses (0-10 for mood, 0-5 for life satisfaction, 0-4 for exercise usefulness) and free-text responses processed by NLP models. Constrained dialogue via decision tree branching. Daily question 'How do you feel now?' with 0-10 scale. End-of-exercise feedback questions. Emergency numbers provided for extreme cases.
quotes:
“Every day, participants received a message from the chatbot asking: "How do you feel now?" Participants could answer the question via a Likert scale from 0 (very bad) to 10 (very good).”
“The users' responses activate various natural language processing (NLP) models, including intention identification, emotion and polarity classifiers”
“For the duration of the non-clinical trial, the feature of providing emergency numbers for local mental health services in extreme cases was introduced.”

title: Does the AI-driven chatbot work? Effectiveness of the Woebot app in reducing anxiety and depression in group counseling courses and student acceptance of technological aids. [References].
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input - users can initiate free dialogues with Woebot or respond to its questions. Each session begins with Woebot asking about the topic of conversation and the user's current mood. Text and emoji responses. Users found responses standardized and lacking true conversational engagement.
quotes:
“Each session begins with Woebot asking about the topic of conversation and the user's current mood. Users can also initiate free dialogues with Woebot”
“using text and emojis to help users address mental health issues”
“its responses weren't truly engaging in a conversation with me. They felt very standardized”
age_as_reported: average age of 26.12 years

title: A Web-Based Stratified Stepped Care Platform for Mental Well-being (TourHeart+): User-Centered Research and Design.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Interactive chatbot format and typeform format options; users can navigate content, access tips and FAQs through 'Got question?' button; emphasis on user autonomy to start, skip, and schedule exercises
quotes:
“chatbot format was deemed more interesting”
“tips and frequently asked questions can be grouped and accessed on every page throughout the exercise through a "Got question?" button”
“the course design should maximize the autonomy of users to start, skip, and schedule any exercises based on their readiness to practice”
age_as_reported: aged between 18 and 60 years and in the work force (interviews); usability testing participants aged 15 to 50+

title: Designing Personality-Adaptive Conversational Agents for Mental Health Care.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input: text and/or voice via CUI. Open-ended conversational dialogue with personality-adaptive language cues. Users can choose social role (friend, therapist), communication style (formal/informal, calm/soothing, witty/humorous, confident/firm, provocative), and degree of anthropomorphism. The PACA can switch social roles within a session. Tone and persona are adaptable to user personality. The conversational design is co-developed by a conversational designer and a therapist. No specific mention of response length, reflection/summarisation, or skip/revise/stop options.
quotes:
“The bot service is responsible for the logical interaction with the user, and therefore is able to process natural language. In addition, the bot service can adapt its conversational design, which determines the style of communication and personality adaptivity (DP6).”
“The conversational design is usually created by a conversational designer, who should co-develop it with a therapist in the case of a PACA.”
“the PACA should be able to change its social role situationally, even within one session”
loc: Section 5.3 Expository Instantiation; Section 5.2 DP4 evaluation
age_as_reported: between 23 and 71 years old, with an average age of 36 years

title: Are online mental health interventions for youth effective? A systematic review.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: AI-based chatbots used text-based conversational interfaces (e.g., MYLO, ELIZA, Woebot, Tess). Web-based synchronous chat involved individual real-time chat sessions with psychotherapists. Web-based self-help platforms comprised modules with psychoeducation and skills training, some including video materials, discussion forums, and guided videoconferences.
quotes:
“Three studies used artificial intelligence-based conversational agents”
“ELIZA is a text-based chatbot designed to encourage users to discuss their problems.”
“Fully automated text-based conversational agent (Weobot)”
“The intervention consisted of individual real-time chat sessions with a psychotherapist”
“Web-based platform: Video-based modules, peer-to-peer discussion forums, brief guided videoconferences”

title: Factors influencing patient engagement in mental health chatbots: A thematic analysis of findings from a systematic review of reviews.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Input and output modalities (written language only or combination of written, spoken, and visual languages), dialog initiative (whether chatbot controls conversation or allows user initiative), interactivity features (asking questions, receiving feedback), verbal and nonverbal behavior simulation, embodiment via avatar or voice
quotes:
“Input and output modalities: The input and output modalities used by the chatbot, such as written language only or a combination of written, spoken, and visual languages, can influence engagement”
“Dialog initiative: Whether the chatbot controls and leads the conversation or allows the user to take the initiative can affect engagement”
“Interactive features, such as the ability to ask questions and receive feedback, can enhance user engagement”

title: "Like I'm Talking to a Real Person": Exploring the Meaning of Transference for the Use and Design of AI-Based Applications in Psychotherapy.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Text-based interaction; chatbot probes users to explore emotions/thought patterns, suggests relaxation exercises, offers techniques and advice; aims to mimic human therapist; pre-scripted regular check-ins
quotes:
“text-based chatbot”
“Many such applications respond to the user in a way that aims to mimic a human therapist, probing the user to explore emotions or thought patterns”
“the chatbot checks in regularly to ask how she is doing, helps her to identify the emotions she feels in difficult situations, and suggests some relaxation exercises to work through her anxiety”

title: Application of Synchronous Text-Based Dialogue Systems in Mental Health Interventions: Systematic Review.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Text-based synchronous chat with free-text exchange of messages mimicking spoken dialogue. Pre-developed responses reusable across clients. Reduced availability of conversational cues (no intonation, nonverbal communication). Slower communication channel: approximately 32 words per minute (chat) versus 143 words per minute in telephone conversation.
quotes:
“text-based communication over the Web that allows participants to rapidly exchange messages, and thereby, mimics spoken dialog”
“the utilization of pre-developed responses that could be reused in conversation with different clients”
“reduced availability of conversational cues during text-based communication, such as the absence of intonation and other nonverbal communication”
“an average of 32 words a minute (chat) versus 143 words a minute in the telephone conversation”
“text-based exchanges generated approximately half the words of an oral conversation”
age_as_reported: Participant ages ranged across the lifespan with 5 studies testing interventions in child or adolescents samples (S3, S5, S6, S8, and S10), 3 in adolescent or adults (S2, S4, and S14), and 5 studies focused exclusively on adults (S1, S7, S9, S11, and S12)

title: A Relational Agent Intervention for Adolescents Seeking Mental Health Treatment: outcomes From a Randomized Controlled Trial Within a Children's Outpatient Hospital
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Text-based conversation with both natural language processing algorithms at free-text entries and forced-choice button replies, with check-ins to confirm understanding and motivation for next steps
quotes: “Conversations are supported by both natural language–processing algorithms at free-text entries as well as forced-choice button replies, with check-ins to conﬁrm understanding and motivation for next steps”
age_as_reported: 13 to 17 years of age

title: SleepPathfinder: A Socratic Questioning and Self-Decision-Based Chatbot to Support User Engagement in Digital CBT-I: Usability and Feasibility Study.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input: button-based selection (education stage, self-decision stage) and free-text multiturn dialogue (Socratic questioning stage). Socratic questioning uses open-ended questions across 5 categories (clarification, assumption probing, evidence exploration, consequence exploration, alternative exploration). Model generates structured outputs: empathic acknowledgment, question type, subquestion, and depth-control signal. Tone: empathic acknowledgment followed by probing questions encouraging hypothesis testing rather than directive correction. Users may accept, defer, or select alternative technique. Advice provision delivers technique-specific guidance grounded in retrieved counseling cases.
quotes:
“an interface layer that enables interaction through button-based selection and multiturn dialogue”
“The model generates structured outputs consisting of empathic acknowledgment, question type, subquestion, and a depth-control signal, supporting conversational continuity while encouraging hypothesis testing rather than directive correction”
“Users may accept the system's recommendation or freely select an alternative CBT-I technique without restriction.”
loc: Methods, System Overview, p.3; Socratic Questioning, p.4; Self-Decision, p.5
age_as_reported: Pilot: mean age 27.4, SD 8.5 years; Experimental: mean age 26.4, SD 3.7 years; undergraduate and graduate students

title: Therapeutic Interaction Features of AI Chatbots in Depression Interventions: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Conversational interaction with sustained, multi-turn dialogue forming the core therapeutic mechanism; structured and guided conversational flows to maintain clarity and therapeutic focus; empathetic responses; feedback mechanisms
quotes:
“sustained, multi-turn dialogue, which forms the core therapeutic mechanism”
“structured and guided conversational flows to maintain clarity and therapeutic focus”

title: Exploring the Application of AI and Extended Reality Technologies in Metaverse-Driven Mental Health Solutions: Scoping Review.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Natural language processing for structured, evidence-based interventions; chatbots use text-based communication with pattern recognition in text and emojis; voice, gesture, and emotional recognition technologies; multimodal understanding of voice, gestures, and avatar behaviors; avatars with nonverbal immediacy behavior enhance rapport; higher human-like interaction increases intention to use via perceived anthropomorphism
quotes:
“AI-powered psychotherapy chatbots (eg, Woebot, Wysa, and Joyable) leverage natural language processing to deliver structured, evidence-based interventions”

title: Conversational Agents in Health Care: Scoping Review of Their Behavior Change Techniques and Underpinning Theory.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Dialog modality: predetermined text (28/47, 60%), free text (8/47, 17%), predetermined and free text (7/47, 15%), not specified (4/47, 9%). 36/47 (77%) displayed a 'coach-like' personality (encouraging, motivating, nurturing); 9/47 (19%) 'health care professional-like'. 27/47 (57%) presented as female agents; 41/47 (87%) responded to a name.
quotes:
“Most CAs (41/47, 87%) responded to a name, 27/47 CAs (57%) were presented as female agents”
“Almost 80% of all CAs (36/47, 77%) displayed a "coach-like" personality, characterized by an encouraging, motivating, and nurturing conversational style”

title: Mind Meets Machine: A Narrative Review of Artificial Intelligence Role in Clinical Psychology Practice. [Review]

title: An overview of the features of chatbots in mental health: A scoping review.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Dialogue initiative: chatbot-led in 87% of studies, mixed in 7 studies. Rule-based chatbots restrict user input to predefined words and phrases. Input modalities: written, spoken, visual, or combinations. Virtual representations (avatars/virtual humans) in 83% of studies.

“In 87% of the included studies, chatbots led and controlled the conversation”
“users of rule-based chatbots cannot usually control the dialogue because their inputs are restricted to predefined words and phrases”
“In 44 studies (83%), virtual representations (e.g. avatar or virtual human) were embodied in chatbots”

value: Free-text, menu-based and mixed input; conversational interfaces with varying degrees of constraint; audio, text, and multimedia response formats; natural conversational flow in voice-based systems
quotes:
“audio/voice interfaces may reduce literacy and motor demands and allow more natural conversational flow”
“voice-based designs”
“text-based interventions”
“multimedia interventions”

title: Development of a Mobile Intervention for Procrastination Augmented With a Semigenerative Chatbot for University Students: pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input: free-text user responses classified by the answer classifier into uncertain, skeptical, or normal categories. Scenario-based dialogue with predetermined questions; generative responses within each scenario step. Interrogative sentences from the generator prompt further user response; declarative sentences advance to the next scenario step. Tone described as 'cute and friendly' by users. Chatbot provides advice, feedback, consolation/cheering, and conversation for reflection. Users can disagree with inferred procrastination factors, triggering alternative advice.
quotes:
“the answer classifier classifies the user's response into 1 of 3 categories: "uncertain," "skeptical," or "normal."”
“When an interrogative sentence is generated, the algorithm waits for the subsequent response from the user. Conversely, in the case of a declarative sentence, the algorithm proceeds to the subsequent step in the scenario.”
“"The cute and friendly tone made me feel comfortable, allowing me to have conversations with Moa with ease"”
loc: Methods, Response-Generating Algorithm; Results, Exploration of User Experience

title: Effectiveness and Safety of Using Chatbots to Improve Mental Health: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
label: Interaction and conversational design

value: Mixed input: primarily menu-based using predetermined text and emoji responses called 'quick replies'; some free-text input when indicated by Writing Hand emoji; constrained dialogue following set pathway with validation branches; short messages favoured; conversational tone with multimedia (GIFs, images, videos, text)
quotes:
“Participants interacted with the chatbot by choosing predetermined text and emojis responses called "quick replies"”
“When a message from Otis was followed by a Writing Hand emoji, this indicated to the user that they could type their own message rather than use a quick reply”
“To simulate empathy, some quick replies prompted specific validation that diverged from the pathway to form the "branches" of the tree before eventually converging back to the main script”
“the delivery of information in short "check-ins" and short messages was favored by the participants”
age_as_reported: Participants aged 18 years and older; actual sample ranged 21–80 years (mean 37.4, SD 15.1)

title: A Therapeutic Conversational Agent (Solace) for Management of Chronic Pain: Acceptability and Usability Study.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input: free-text field or selectable starter prompts. User inputs accepted without restrictions on length or content. Open-ended engagement encouraged. Responses typically 1-4 sentences (average 49.73 words). Empathic responses embedded throughout. Plain language. Therapeutic guidance toward evidence-based strategies.
quotes:
“Users began their experience with Solace by typing freely or selecting from starter prompts”
“User inputs were accepted without restrictions on length or content.”
“Open-ended engagement, encouraging users to freely express their thoughts and emotions”
“Emotional sensitivity, with empathic responses embedded throughout the conversation”
“were presented to the user as (typically) 1-4 sentences”
“Plain language to ensure accessibility and reduce cognitive burden”
loc: Methods - Conversational Design and Rules section; Results - Usage Characteristics
age_as_reported: 18 years of age or older

title: A Chatbot-Based Coaching Intervention for Adolescents to Promote Life Skills: Pilot Study.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input: users type free-text responses to chatbot questions and choose from options (e.g., emotion guessing game). Open-ended dialogue with constrained pathways. Chatbot persona is an older peer with friendly, coaching tone. Chatbot asks questions, proposes exercises for self-reflection, and provides advice via video cartoons. Users noted some dialogue unclear, lack of empathy, too much text requiring scrolling, and redundancy in longer sessions.
quotes:
“The chatbot then continues the conversation by asking questions and proposing exercises to trigger user self-reflection on how to cope and behave in such a situation”
“the need to type answers during the chat when replying to the chatbot's questions helped them to reflect on their feelings and thoughts”
“Let's exercise by playing a game! I'll show you an emotion, you guess which one it is by choosing one of three options.”
“I like this chatbot, he looks like a boy, just a bit older than me, but not an adult; he is sensitive and very smart.”
“When the bot sends too much text in a turn, I need to scroll up not to miss the first lines and this is a bit annoying.”
age_as_reported: age range of 12-17 years (mean 14.52)

title: A review of artificial intelligence enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy using the BECK AI BOT for mental health interventions.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Text-based conversational input; RASA pipeline for intent detection and entity identification; user inputs classified into categories like stress expression, negative automatic thoughts, crisis signals; MentalBERT provides cognitive distortion detection
quotes:
“Natural language comprehension is managed by a RASA-driven pipeline that executes detection and entity identification”
“User inputs are sorted into relevant classes, such as stress expression, negative automatic thoughts, avoidance actions”

title: Self-Guided Web-Based Interventions: Scoping Review on User Needs and the Potential of Embodied Conversational Agents to Address Them.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Both closed (menu-based, predefined options) and open dialogue (free text or free speech) discussed. ECAs enable multiple question-and-answer pairs. Open dialogue can lead to off-topic questions. Short dialogues recommended to maintain credibility. ECA should communicate intention, capabilities, and limitations and behave consistently. Users should have control over ECA presence. Empathy and humor in conversation style mentioned.
quotes:
“ECAs enable more open-ended and more relationship-oriented interactions. Interactions between ECAs and users can span multiple question-and-answer pairs”
“a robot taking the role of a museum guide who uses, for example, empathy and humor in his conversation style”
“In such a closed dialogue scenario, the interactions between the user and the software traditionally have a task-specific character”
“it is recommended that the ECA has short dialogues with the user. Systems that permit longer open-ended dialogues are playfully tested [52]. By limiting the scope and length of the dialogues, the ECA will more likely keep up its credibility.”

title: Designing Chatbots to Treat Depression in Youth: Qualitative Study.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input: primarily menu-based with predefined button options, free-text input allowed in specific situations (e.g., identifying pleasant activities). Chatbot used emojis and GIFs in messages. Free-text responses did not alter conversation pathway.
quotes:
“users primarily interacted with the chatbot by selecting from predefined options presented as buttons. We allowed free-text input in specific situations, for example, to identify and schedule pleasant activities”
“Cady also used emojis in its messages and sent GIFs”
age_as_reported: 14-17 years old

title: What Role Can Avatars Play in e-Mental Health Interventions? Exploring New Models of Client-Therapist Interaction. [Review]
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input modes: text and/or audio in Second Life; avatar-mediated symbolic expression (ProReal with virtual props); SPARX uses game-like interaction with automated guide providing tasks and summaries; autonomous agents (Ellie) respond to text-based, auditory, and/or sensory input. Tone described as warm and caring for SPARX automated characters. Participant feedback requested greater range of user input and avatar response options.
quotes:
“remotely interact with other users – also represented as avatars – via text and/or audio”
“ProReal avatars can also be given virtual props to facilitate symbolic emotional expression”
“At the commencement of each module, participants meet with an automated guide whose role is akin to a therapist”
“automated characters that were perceived as being warm and caring”
“Participant feedback for future versions of the intervention included greater range of user input and avatar response options”
loc: Applications section, p.2-4; Online Peer Support Communities section, p.2; Avatars to Participate in Serious Games section, p.3; Avatars as Autonomous Virtual Therapists section, p.3

title: Digital conversational agents for youth with multiple mental health conditions: A qualitative descriptive study of youth perspectives on the acceptability, potential benefits, and challenges. [References].

value: Conversational interaction; can chat like a friend or clinician; can share information about mental health, resources, or coping skills, or just ask how your day was; emulates empathy in responses
quotes:
“it can chat like a friend, or it can chat like a clinician. It can share information about mental health, or resources, or coping skills – or, it can just ask how your day was.”
“Then it emulates empathy as it responds to you.”

title: The role of artificial intelligence in mental health: a comprehensive review.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Conversational interactions that simulate human interactions; user feedback has led to improvements in tone and conversational flow; limitations include absence of nonverbal cues, shared context, and nuanced emotional reciprocity
quotes:
“simulate human interactions”
“user feedback has led to improvements in the tone and conversational flow of popular mental health chatbots.”
“The absence of nonverbal cues, shared context, and nuanced emotional reciprocity in AI interactions can undermine relational trust”

title: Conversational agents for depression screening: A systematic review.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Interaction types include text-based chat, voice-based dialogue, and combined text/voice/video. Some CAs use free-text input (e.g., Wysa described as 'Free-Text CBT Conversational Agent'). Most text-based CAs use chat interfaces. Voice CAs use ASR and TTS. The review notes voice interaction is 'perceived as more natural and less invasive.'
quotes:
“The interaction implemented in most relevant conversational agents is text-based”
“voice interaction is perceived as more natural and less invasive”
“Evaluating the Therapeutic Alliance with a Free-Text CBT Conversational Agent (Wysa)”

title: Early detection of depression using a conversational AI bot: A non-clinical trial
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Open-ended free-text input (multiple choice removed); constrained dialogue following fixed HIG sequence; 27 questions presented sequentially; dynamic responses via fulfillment functions; participants can express thoughts spontaneously; clinical/structured interview tone
quotes:
“DEPRA eliminates dependence on a limited set of multiple-choice replies in favour of open-ended responses, allowing participants to express their thoughts and sentiments spontaneously and without hesitation”
“removes multiple choice, sub-questions, and questions with conditional statements”
“To provide a dynamic response, we validate the response received from the user, store it in the central database and define a number of functions in the fulfillment.”
loc: Methods p.6, p.9; Architecture of DEPRA, p.8

title: User perceptions and utilisation of features of an AI-enabled workplace digital mental wellness platform 'mindline at work'.
label: Interaction and conversational design
value: Mixed input: free-form text conversation with Wysa chatbot; menu-based selection for multimedia resources and mood check-in (limited mood options). Wysa provides structured perspectives, frameworks, and reflection. Anonymous, non-judgmental tone. Some participants noted limited mood selection options.
quotes:
“individuals seeking 'human interaction' can engage in free-­form conversation and digital therapeutics exercises with Wysa in a safe and anonymous manner”
“some participants, although not many, expressed discontent with the limited options available for mood selection, which diminished their overall user experience”
“Wysa puts words into perspective, puts a framework to user experience, and helps users recognize that: Hey, you are not alone!”

title: Challenges in Implementing a Mobile AI Chatbot Intervention for Depression Among Youth on Psychiatric Waiting Lists: a Randomized Control Study Termination Report
label: Human-support model
value: Fully automated chatbot intervention with minimal human support limited to assessment and monitoring. Non-physician research assistants conducted weekly online assessments, performed minimal mental status checks, and provided technical assistance. No direct involvement in the therapeutic process. For routine application outside the RCT, no human involvement would be required
quotes:
“Human support was limited to assessment and monitoring during the intervention, with no direct involvement in the therapeutic process”
“The periodic assessments were administered by non physician research assistants, who performed minimal mental status checks”
“For routine application outside of the RCT setting, no human involvement would be required”

title: Mental Distress, Label Avoidance, and Use of a Mental Health Chatbot: Results From a US Survey.
label: Human-support model
value: Fully automated - no human involvement during chatbot interaction. Chatbot provides crisis line numbers for higher distress levels but does not connect to a human.
quotes:
“making clear that—despite the human-like nature of the text messages—it was a computer program and not a human responding.”
“Tabatha provided users with phone numbers for emergency services if they were experiencing a crisis.”

title: Large Language Models for Mental Health Applications: Systematic Review.
label: Human-support model
value: The review emphasises that LLMs should augment, not replace, human practitioners. LLMs described as requiring professional oversight. Fully automated with recommendations for professional oversight; not intended as substitutes for professional mental health services.
quotes:
“AI tools should augment, rather than replace, human practitioners”
“LLMs require professional oversight and should not be used independently. Nevertheless, when used as decision aids, LLMs have the potential to enhance health care efficiency”

title: Providers of relief in distress: RAG-based LLMs as situation and intent-aware assistants.
label: Human-support model
value: Fully automated; no human support component in current version. Human-in-the-loop escalation for high-risk conversations (e.g., suicidal intent, abuse) is planned as future work. System includes safety disclaimers and directs users to emergency services (911, 988) but does not route to a human.
quotes:
“LLooMi could implement a mechanism for contextual handoﬀ, allowing it to route certain users to a qualiﬁed professional.”
“users facing urgent or life-threatening crises are strongly advised to contact local emergency services (e.g., 911 in the U.S.) or mental health crisis hotlines such as the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (988).”

title: Chatbot-Delivered Interventions for Improving Mental Health Among Young People: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
label: Human-support model
value: Most chatbots were fully automated. Only 3 studies explicitly integrated human assistance (Bray et al. 2020; Nicol et al. 2022; Russell et al. 2021) and showed lower attrition rates. Safety measures included emergency assistance (n=12), crisis identification (n=6), and professional accompaniment (n=2). Review notes safety concerns from fully automated nature.
quotes:
“only three included studies explicitly mentioned integrating human assistance into the chatbot and showed lower attrition rates (Bray et al. 2020; Nicol et al. 2022; Russell et al. 2021)”
“encompassing emergency assistance (n = 12), crisis identification (n = 6), and professional accompaniment (n = 2)”
“the fully automated nature of chatbots in mental health care may raise safety concerns, such as limited capacity to monitor and address negative emotional reactions during interventions”

age_as_reported: young people aged between 10 and 24 years; included studies varied from 8 to 33 years

quotes:
“If a user reported suicidal ideation via the PHQ-9 questionnaire or if the conversational agent detected suicide-related content in conversations, an alert was triggered to notify the research team”
“An emergency alert system triggers an email alert for the clinical team to make immediate contact in critical situations”

title: BetterMood: A human-like AI counseling service for adolescents and young adults.

Authors suggest safety guardrails for crisis triage and escalation to human professionals as a policy recommendation, but this is not implemented in the current system.
quotes:
“Additionally, the professional clinicians participate in counseling sessions using BetterMood and provide evaluations from an expert perspective”
“they could mandate the implementation of safety guardrails that effectively triage crisis situations and escalate them to human professionals.”

“for the intervention to be truly effective, it must be supported by a structured programme involving a professional”
“We also envisage a stepped-care model that integrates midwives and mental health professionals for triage and escalation when risk flags are detected.”
